blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Face verification is central to Automated Border Control (ABC), where a live
capture is compared with the face image stored in an electronic
machine-readable travel document [ 13 ] . This process
assumes that the document image represents one genuine identity. Face morphing
attacks violate this assumption by combining information from two contributors,
allowing both to resemble the document photograph during enrolment or later
verification [ 4 , 1 ] . Such attacks can be
produced through landmark-based blending [ 12 ] , GAN-based
synthesis [ 25 ] , and diffusion-based
generation [ 26 ] .

blocks.en:
Single-image MAD examines a document image in isolation, whereas Differential
MAD (D-MAD) compares it with a trusted live capture. The differential setting
provides identity evidence that is unavailable in single-image inspection and
therefore fits the ABC workflow. Most D-MAD methods nevertheless require
labelled morph pairs to train a classifier or adapt a pretrained
representation [ 2 , 8 ] . Their
development is constrained by limited biometric data and by the difficulty of
covering morph generation and acquisition conditions that may arise after
deployment.

blocks.en:
A frozen-parameter Vision-Language Model (VLM) offers a complementary approach
because it can compare two facial images without model fine-tuning. Existing
studies demonstrate zero-shot MAD and related presentation attack detection
with manually defined prompts [ 1 , 27 , 19 , 11 ] . Prompt choice therefore remains an uncontrolled
experimental factor. Within VLM-based MAD, no subject-disjoint validation rule
has been studied for selecting among alternatives. Our procedure uses
validation labels and is supervised prompt selection, although no model
parameters are updated.

blocks.en:
We treat prompt design as a controlled D-MAD variable. Version 1 generates 50
candidates, ranks them on a validation split with disjoint subjects, and fixes
the top-ranked prompt before testing. Version 2 starts from 30 Generation 0
prompts and revises selected candidates using aggregate validation feedback.
Both variants minimise the security loss ℒ sec \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sec}} , which
prioritises missed attack reduction while accounting for bona fide errors and
response reliability. The evaluator configuration is held constant within each
comparison, and no test image, label, or metric contributes to prompt
generation or selection.

blocks.en:
The main contributions of this work are: 1. We instantiate prompt design as a validation-guided selection problem
and compare a manual prompt, non-recursive selection, and recursive
optimisation under the same frozen-parameter evaluator configuration and
test protocol. 2. We define a failure-aware evaluation protocol with MACER-oriented
prompt ranking, OR decision fusion, maximum morph-risk-score fusion, and
explicit handling of response and parse failures. 3. We evaluate subject-disjoint bona fide and morph pairs covering different morphing generation techniques such as LMA [ 7 ] ,
MIPGAN-2 [ 25 ] , and PIPE [ 26 ] , with analyses of morph-specific errors, response budget,
subject-level uncertainty, and recursive optimisation behaviour.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Conventional D-MAD. Early differential approaches compare facial representations extracted
from the document image and live capture. The resulting feature difference
or similarity is evaluated directly or passed to a lightweight classifier
such as an SVM [ 22 , 10 , 13 ] . These methods benefit
from identity information in the trusted reference image, but their
performance depends on the representation model, the training attacks,
and the availability of labelled morph pairs. De-morphing methods instead
estimate and remove the live capture contribution before testing whether
the residual is compatible with another identity [ 6 , 9 ] . Their behaviour can
depend on assumptions about the blending process and the quality of the
input images.

blocks.en:
Prompt design in biometric security. Recent work explores prompting multimodal models for biometric tasks. Zhang
et al. [ 27 ] use designed prompts for zero-shot MAD;
Shekhawat et al. [ 1 ] extend this to D-MAD with
chain-of-thought instructions; Patwardhan et al. [ 19 ] compare
manually written prompts; and Narayan et al. [ 14 ] evaluate zero-shot, task-description, and chain-of-thought prompting across
face tasks. These studies show prompt sensitivity but do not select an
instruction using subject-disjoint labelled validation data. General prompt
optimisation generates, selects, or iteratively refines instructions [ 28 , 24 , 20 ] . We instead treat prompt choice
as a controlled D-MAD variable: candidates are ranked on subject-disjoint
validation data and frozen before test evaluation. Thus, our contribution is
supervised black-box prompt selection for D-MAD, not a new general
prompt-optimisation algorithm.

Version 1 examines whether prompt selection based on validation performance can improve a frozen-parameter VLM evaluator without recursive prompt revision. The Prompt Generator Agent produces 50 complete candidate prompts from a common D-MAD task description, output schema, and set of content constraints. The candidates differ in their emphasis on facial geometry, local identity
consistency, visible morphing artefacts, image quality, and final decision
formulation. During evaluation, every candidate is combined with the same evaluator model, system instruction, image role description, JSON schema, and inference settings. This design isolates the effect of the candidate prompt while keeping the remaining components fixed.

generation and revision use a temperature of 0.8 to encourage variation,
whereas prompt evaluation and critic screening use a temperature of zero.
Repeated calls at temperature zero are treated as separate observations rather

blocks.en: 5 Limitations and Future Work
blocks.zh: 5. 限制和今后的工作

blocks.en:
The study uses one VLM configuration without parameter updates and one dataset
with disjoint validation and test subjects. This scope follows the consent
constraints of Section 4.1 ; the other considered benchmarks did
not authorise external processing of identifiable facial images. Transfer
across models, datasets, demographics, morph generators, and acquisition
conditions is therefore untested. The validation split of 10 subjects may
overfit prompt selection, while the mutable API alias limits temporal
reproducibility. No ablation removes or mismatches the trusted reference, so
the use of differential rather than document image evidence remains
unquantified. The visual references use a common uncalibrated threshold, and
the VLM risk scores are also uncalibrated. For consequential D-MAD decisions,
VLM outputs should only assist trained human review. External processing must
follow applicable consent, access, retention, and jurisdictional requirements.
We redistribute no images or subject identifiers.

blocks.en:
The Version 1 prompt selected on validation data obtains 19.17 % 19.17\% MACER,
compared with 70.00 % 70.00\% for the manual prompt, at 0.00 % 0.00\% observed
BSCER. It has fewer missed attacks for 37 of 40 test subjects, with no reverse
outcome. Recursive optimisation does not improve the best Generation 0
validation loss; its reported descendant obtains 31.67 % 31.67\% test MACER.
Errors remain concentrated in LMA. These results show that prompt formulation
can have a substantial effect on the behaviour of a frozen VLM in D-MAD and
should therefore be treated as part of the evaluation protocol rather than as
a minor implementation choice. At the same time, the remaining LMA errors
suggest that relying mainly on visible blending and texture cues is not enough
for more challenging morphs, and that stronger use of differential identity
evidence may be needed. The findings are limited to the model and dataset
studied here and should not be interpreted as general superiority across
D-MAD systems. Future work should examine reference image use and transfer
across models and datasets while retaining human oversight.

blocks.en:
After the anonymous review process, the reproducibility package will contain
the 50 Version 1 prompts and rankings; the Generation 0–2 populations and
lineage fields; the frozen P033 and G1_P014 records; the
manual instruction; parsing, fusion, metric, bootstrap, and ablation scripts;
de-identified outputs; and a README specifying the response schema, split
sizes, model alias, temperatures, and procedure.

The release excludes API credentials, raw facial images, image paths, and
direct subject identifiers. External processing of identifiable facial images
must comply with the consent, access, retention, and processing conditions of
the source collection and deployment jurisdiction. The reported system is
intended only to assist trained document inspection personnel and should not
serve as the sole basis for a consequential identity decision.
